tips.title: body set up sheet
tips.text:
- Set the clearance plane to 2.0 inches for all operations to ensure adequate tool clearance.
- Use a retract plane of 0.25 inches for most milling operations to prevent collision with workpiece.
- For high-speed surface roughing, maintain a spindle speed of 6112 RPM and feedrate of 36.672 inch/min for optimal material removal rate.
- When drilling, ensure the spindle speed is set to 764 RPM and feedrate to 3.056 inch/min to avoid tool breakage on harder materials.
- For facing operations, use a spindle speed of 1673 RPM and feedrate of 23.422 inch/min for efficient stock removal.
- In contour milling, adjust the feed plane to 0.2 inches and maintain a retract plane of 0.25 inches to ensure smooth cutting action.
- Use a peck drill with a depth of -0.9874 inches and spindle speed of 764 RPM for deep holes to prevent tool overheating.
- For finish milling, reduce the feedrate to match the spindle speed to achieve a finer surface finish without excessive heat generation.

tips.title: mori-atc38-50t-installation-maintenance
tips.text:

- Verify motor rotation direction matches the directional arrow on the hydraulic pump casing.
- Bleed air from the pump by starting and stopping the motor 5 to 6 times initially.
- Adjust flowrate to 8 gpm using the horizontal screw with lock-nut, ensuring no-load state.

tips.title: InventorCAM2024_5-Axis_Basic_Training_Vol-2
tips.text:
- Ensure the geometry for morphing is selected directly from drive surfaces to avoid errors in tool path generation.
- Set the tilt angle at side of cutting carefully (e.g., 70 degrees) to prevent rubbing on steep areas like impeller blades.
- Use Lead-In and Lead-Out parameters precisely to control entry and exit points, enhancing tool life and surface finish.
- Enable gouge checking with Retract tool and Along tool axis strategies to prevent collisions during machining.
- Adjust the small move size in links (e.g., 500% of step over) to ensure smooth transitions between tool paths.
- Calculate margins accurately to avoid cutting too close to edges, which can cause chipping or poor finish.
- Use different side tilt definitions like Orthogonal and Follow surface ISO Lines direction for varied machining scenarios.
- Simulate tool paths thoroughly before finalizing operations to catch any issues related to geometry selection or parameter settings.

tips.title: Feeds and Speeds Explained: A Beginner's Guide for Machinists
tips.text:
- Feeds and Speeds Measurement: Feeds are measured in inches per minute, indicating how fast the tool travels across the material.
- Difference Between Lathe and Mill Feeds: On a lathe, the spindle spins the material while the tool is stationary; on a mill, the tool in the spindle moves across the material held in a vice.
- Safety Importance of Feeds and Speeds: Incorrect feeds and speeds can lead to machine crashes, injuries, or damage to the shop.
- Time and Money Importance of Feeds and Speeds: Proper feeds and speeds can significantly reduce machining time, improving efficiency and cost-effectiveness.
- Stress in Material: Using incorrect feeds and speeds can introduce stress into the material, which can cause issues during heat treatment or other post-processing steps.
- Feeds and Speeds Importance: Proper feeds and speeds are crucial to avoid stress in the material, ensuring better quality parts after heat treatment.
- Variability in Machining: Different machinists may use different feeds and speeds, leading to variability in the machining process even with identical setups.
- Follow Manufacturer Recommendations: If you buy tools from manufacturers like Inol or Kental, refer to their website for charts displaying recommended speeds and feeds. These recommendations are usually displayed on charts that we will cover how to understand.
- Start with Manufacturing Settings: If you're in a bind and need to get started, use the manufacturing settings as a starting point.
- Use HSM Advisor or FS Wizard: These tools can help you get started by providing recommendations based on your tool, material, and coolant.
- Know Your Material: Research the material's machineability and choose appropriate coolant and tool type.
- Setup Matters: A weak setup can cause issues even if feeds and speeds are correct.
- Adjust Feed Rate Based on Setup: Start around 50-70% of the recommended feed rate and adjust based on sound and experience.
- Adjusting Feeds and Speeds by Ear: Adjust feeds and speeds based on sound; if it sounds like 'poop', slow the feed rate or spindle speed.
- Chatter and Feed Rate Adjustment: If there's chatter, try slowing the feed rate or adjusting the tool holder position slightly.

tips.title: Quick Machining Tip #9 - Conventional and Climb Milling
tips.text:
- Conventional Milling Feed Direction: In conventional milling, the feed of the part goes in the opposite direction of the rotation of the cutter.
- Benefits of Conventional Milling on Manual Machines: Conventional milling loads the lead screw in the correct direction against the nut, which is beneficial for manual machines.
- Climb Milling Feed Direction: In climb milling, the feed of the part goes in the same direction as the rotation of the cutter.
- Potential Issues with Climb Milling on Manual Machines: Climb milling can cause the lead screw to be pushed away from the nut, potentially leading to backlash issues and violent cutter force.
- Surface Finish Comparison: Climb milling leaves a better surface finish compared to conventional milling.
- Changing Milling Direction: You cannot change between climb and conventional milling by reversing the cutter's rotation; you must change the direction of feed.
- Conventional Milling Chip Management: Chips in conventional milling tend to get swept back into the cutter and recut, affecting surface finish.
- Surface Finish Improvement with Climb Milling: Climb milling results in a significantly better surface finish compared to conventional milling, especially on CNC machines without backlash issues.
- Backlash Issues in Conventional Milling: Conventional milling on manual machines with backlash can destroy parts or cutters during climb cuts, whereas CNC machines with ball screws typically do not have this issue.
- Light Climb Cut for Aluminum Finishing: A very light climb cut (about five thousandths of an inch) is effective for improving surface finish on aluminum after conventional milling.

tips.title: How To Use Depth Of Cut For Max Endmill SPEEDS & FEEDS
tips.text:
- End Mill Cutting Parameters: Modern high performance end mills work best with correct cutting parameters to achieve high quality parts efficiently.
- Depth of Cut Explanation: An end mill cuts with the side and end face; step over uses the side, step down uses the end face.
- Step Over and Step Down: Step over is radial depth of cut or optimal load step over, while step down is axial depth of cut corresponding to z-axis travel.
- Even Steps for Constant Force: Taking even steps keeps constant force on the tool and removes wasted motion.
- Flute Count and Depth of Cut: Tools with less flutes have more distance between cutting edges for increased stepover, while tools with more flutes have less chip space but extra cutting edges.
- Material Suitability for Flute Count: Most 2 and 3 flutes are designed for soft materials like aluminum, while tools with more flutes are designed for hard and abrasive materials.
- Roughing and Finishing Cuts: Roughing removes the bulk of material, while a final cut leaves a smooth finish.

tips.title: Metal Lathe Tutorial 12 : Surface Finish
tips.text:
- Surface Finish Extremes: The extremes of surface finish range from very poor, possibly corroded surfaces to highly polished ones achieved through precision grinding.
- Importance of Surface Finish for Precision: Surface finish affects precision measurements, especially in tight tolerances where tool marks can skew readings.
- Surface Finish in Bearing Fits: Good surface finish is crucial for proper interference fits to avoid damaging components like bearings.
- Surface Finish in Heat Treating: A smooth surface finish aids in visual color assessment during heat tempering, ensuring accurate hardness control.
- Smooth Surface for Cold Bluing: A smooth clean surface is crucial for an accurate cold bluing process.
- Surface Finish and Corrosion Resistance: Better surface finish improves corrosion resistance, reducing flash rust on unprotected steel.
- Evaluating Surface Finish by Feel and Sight: Evaluate surface finish by feeling it and using your fingernail to detect roughness; materials like brass hide tool marks better than steel or aluminum.
- Surface Finish Rule of Thumb: A good surface finish on steel should be smooth and shiny, with the grain of the material being more dominant than tool marks.
- Material Choice Matters: The choice of alloy affects surface finish quality; 12L14 free machining steel has a small amount of lead, making it machine nicely and achieve good chip action.
- Avoid Chatter for Good Surface Finish: Lousy chip action and a bird's nest of chips indicate improper speeds and feeds, leading to a bad surface finish.
- Single Point Cutting Tool Consideration: Lathes are single point cutting tools, meaning only the very tip of the tool is doing the cutting, which creates a helix on the surface.
- Poor Surface Finish Indicators: Little balls or lumps on the surface indicate poor chip action and material not cutting cleanly, leading to burrs and roughness.
- Tool Selection for Surface Finish: A very fine pointed tool is used for thread cutting to achieve a smooth finish, while a round-nose tool can smear the surface and create a nicer finish by averaging out tiny marks.
- Nose Radius Effect on Surface Finish: A round-nose tool with a small nose radius provides a much nicer surface finish by averaging out tiny thread marks, while a sharp tool can lead to poor finishes.
- Tool Pressure and Nose Radius: Larger nose radius increases tool pressure, which can cause chatter. Larger radius tools are reserved for finishing passes with light cuts to avoid chatter.
- Sharp Nose Tools for Minimizing Tool Pressure: Very sharp nose tools are used to minimize tool pressure, which is crucial in certain operations like cutting small parts.
- Use Sharpest Tool for Tough Materials: When machining tough materials like tool steel, use the sharpest tool to prevent chatter.
- Tool Selection for Roughing and Finishing: Use sharp nose tools for roughing to remove material quickly, then switch to a tool with a modest radius for finishing passes.
- Importance of Speeds and Feeds: Surface finish is largely about getting speeds and feeds right, especially with larger tool radii.
- Experiment for Optimal Speeds and Feeds: Experiment in your own shop to find the right surface speed for each material, as books often provide maximum production settings.
- Sharp Tools and Correct Angles: Ensure your tool is sharp and angles are correct for better surface finishes.
- Manipulate Speeds and Feeds for Desired Effect: Adjust speeds and feeds within the desired range to achieve the surface finish effect you want.
- Fine Thread Cutting: The finer the thread, the slower the material and tool should spin to achieve a smooth surface finish.
- Speeds and Feeds for Surface Finish: Higher spindle speed with slower feed rate gives a better surface finish, while lower spindle speed with higher feed rate removes material more efficiently.
- Final Pass for Best Surface Finish: For the best surface finish, use a shallow cut with high spindle speed and slow feed rate.
- Role of Cutting Fluid in Surface Finish: Cutting fluid improves chip control and helps clear chips away from the cutting tool, enhancing surface finish.
- Cutting Fluid for Different Materials: Tap Magic is suitable for steel and softer materials like aluminum, copper, and brass; WD40 can be used in roughing passes to carry heat away.
- Fingernail Test for Surface Finish: The surface passes the fingernail test, meaning no marks can be felt with a fingernail.
- Grinding for Best Surface Finish: The best surface finishes come from using a grinder because the tool marks are microscopic.
- Using Emery Paper for Surface Finishing: Use Emery paper to achieve a smooth surface, starting with 400 grit and progressing to finer grits like 1,000 and 2,000.
- Protecting Lathe Ways from Grit: Always protect the lathe ways when using stone-based tools to prevent grit damage.
- Using Oil During Grinding: Apply a little bit of oil during grinding to keep the sanding area clean and prevent grit from collecting in the paper.
- Be cautious with 400 grit sandpaper: Using 400 grit sandpaper can remove a significant amount of material, potentially up to 3/10 or more off the dimension. Be careful not to get carried away and remove too much.
- Rescue mediocre surface finish with Amry paper: Amry paper can be used to improve a mediocre surface finish.

tips.title: Why Use Hydraulic Tool Holders on CNC Routers
tips.text:
- Hydraulic Tool Holder Torque Setting: Use a torque wrench with a setting of 5.7 newton meters to ensure the hydraulic tool holder is tightly clamped.
- Height Adjustment with Hydraulic Tool Holder: Hydraulic tool holders can be slightly tightened to provide tension, making it easier to set the height without the tool falling.
- Hydraulic Tool Holders Reduce Runout: The hydraulic tool holder's bladder collapses around the shank, providing 360 degrees of radial clamping and reducing runout.
- Better Finishes with Hydraulic Tool Holders: Hydraulic tool holders provide better finishes on materials like plastic due to reduced runout and more consistent flute contact.
- Even Tool Wear with Hydraulic Holders: Hydraulic tool holders lead to even flute wear and longer tool life by ensuring consistent contact.
- Hydraulic Holders for High Feed Rates: Hydraulic tool holders are beneficial for high feed rates and production work, offering consistent parts and longer tool life.

tips.title: Radial Chip Thinning
tips.text:
- Chip Thinning at Center Line: At the center line of the tool path, the chip thickness equals the feed per tooth.
- Chip Thinning Effect on Flutes: As the flutes pass center, the chip gets thinner and exits the cut.
- Width of Cut Impact on Chip Thickness: Reducing the width of cut to less than half the diameter results in thinner chips.
- Compensation for Reduced Chip Thickness: If you reduce the width of cut, you need to compensate by increasing the feed rate.
- Example of Chip Thinning Calculation: For a 1/2 inch 4 flute endmill at 400 surface feet and 4,000 feet per tooth with 5% radial engagement, the correct feed rate is 112 in per minute.
- Heat Consideration with Radial Engagement: Greater radial engagement increases heat, so surface feet should be doubled to get the right amount of heat.
- Importance of Understanding Chip Thinning Geometry: Understanding the geometry behind chip thinning allows for better tool path verification and quick manual corrections.
- Balancing Feed and Radial Engagement: It's about balance to fine-tune your feed to match radial engagement, ensuring every flute cuts efficiently and carries away the right amount of heat.
- Turning Safe Feeds into Optimal Feeds: Balancing feed and radial engagement helps turn safe feeds into optimal feeds, resulting in faster, cooler, and more consistent cuts.

tips.title: Trochoidal Toolpaths Programming Tutorial
tips.text:
- Chip Thinning Effect: When the width of cut is lower than 50% tool diameter, there's a natural chip thinning effect. You need to increase your feed per tooth to maintain your chip load.
- Feed Per Tooth vs Chip Load: Feed per tooth does not equal chip load. You need to use a specific formula or spreadsheet to calculate your feed per tooth considering chip thinning.
- Axial Chip Thinning: Tools with curved cutting edges, such as rounded inserts and ball cutters, can experience axial chip thinning due to lead angle.
- Avoid Conventional Milling in Machine: Conventional milling produces more heat and can weld the chip onto the tool. Only use climb milling unless cutting wood.
- Reduce Feed Rate for Internal Radii: When cutting internal radii, the angle of engagement increases, requiring a reduction in feed rate to account for chip thinning loss.
- Avoid High Centripetal Acceleration: If the centripetal acceleration calculation turns red in the spreadsheet, you need to slow down the feed rate, lower the chip load, reduce the RPM, or increase the ending diameter to prevent the machine from losing accuracy and producing oval shapes instead of circles.
- Setting Up Material Orientation: Ensure the Z-axis is vertical to align with the spindle centerline for proper part orientation.
- Fixing X-Axis Orientation: Select the top edge of a part and flip the X-axis to ensure more material is available for cutting in that direction.
- Setting Fixed Stock Size: Set the stock size to a fixed box with dimensions X=16 inches, Y=12 inches, and Z=0.825 inches based on measured material.
- Offsetting Material Position: Offset the material position from the left side by -0.5 inches in X and from the front side by -0.5 inches in Y to align with the stock box.
- Use 3D Adaptive Toolpath for Critical Features: Rough out important features first, finish them, then do everything else using a 3D adaptive toolpath.
- Spindle Speed Recommendation: Use a spindle speed of 16,000 rpm as recommended by the tool manufacturer and tested for this specific application.
- High Chip Load for Aluminum Machining: Use a high chip load of about 0.046 when cutting 6061 aluminum at 16,000 rpm to ensure the chip has enough thermal mass.
- Chip Heat Management: The chip takes away heat from the tool and material, ensuring that heat does not stay on the cutting surfaces.
- Speed and Feed Rate for 3/16 Cutter: For a 3/16 inch cutter at 16,000 RPM, the recommended surface speed is 785.46 feet per minute with a feed rate of about 104 inches per minute.
- Chip Load Recommendation: The tooling manufacturer recommends a chip load of three to six tabs, and for ramping, it's recommended to go at 50% of the cutting feed rate.
- Avoiding Film and Welding: Ensure the tool goes below the part to avoid leaving a film, which can cause welding.
- Tolerance Setting for Whisper Cuts: Increase the tolerance to half an inch to avoid whisper cuts.
- Smoothing Setting Choke: A smoothing setting of 2000 will choke.
- Horizontal Lead and Lead Out Radius: Set the horizontal lead and lead out radius to 0.075.
- Ramping Angle Recommendation: Use a ramping angle of 10 degrees as recommended.
- Tool Path Generation Monitoring: Select the tool path and go to test manager to see how far it is in generating.
- Bearing Holes Importance: Finish the bearing holes first because they are technically the most important holes on these parts.
- Trochoidal Milling and Accuracy: Trochoidal milling removes large circles with low centripetal acceleration, so the machine won't lose accuracy at about 140 inches a minute.
- Chip Load Adjustment: When finishing with a narrow cut, increase the chip load slightly but avoid going too high as it can break the tool. A chip load of one and a half is too much, so stick to around one.
- Feed Rate for Finishing: For finishing operations, a feed rate of 30 inches per minute at 16,000 RPM is safe and effective.
- Plunge Feed Rate for Finishing: Set the plunge feed rate to 50 inches per minute because the roughing tool path has already moved the material, so no plunging into fresh material is needed.
- Plunge Feed Rate: A slow plunge feed rate (50) can cause delays, so it's better to avoid a very low number.
- Spindle Speed and Feed Rate: The spindle speed is set to 16,000 rpm with a feed rate of 30 inches per minute for lead cutting.
- Lead and Lead Out Radius: Increasing the lead and lead out radius helps reduce central acceleration, making the machine movement gentler.
- Drilling Tool Path Setup: When setting up a drilling tool path, ensure the Z-axis is correctly selected and regenerate the face with flanges to avoid errors in simulation.
- Drill Tool Path Parameters: For drilling, set the minimum diameter to 0.158 and use default maximum diameter. Set feed heights from model top with a breakthrough depth of 30th au.
- Simulation Check for Drilling Path: After setting up the drilling tool path, run a simulation to ensure the tool is targeting the correct holes and not plunging incorrectly.
- Cutting Speed for Trochoidal Toolpaths: The cutting speed was set at 15 inches per minute, which allowed the tool to plunge in and retract as intended.
- Clearance Height Adjustment for Obstacles: If screws or other obstacles were present between parts, the clearance height would need to be raised in the heights tab.
- Breaking Centripetal Acceleration Rule: The operator is breaking the centripetal acceleration rule by increasing the ramp feed rate with a larger diameter, but it is acceptable in this case.
- Rest Machining for Small Holes: Rest machining is enabled to ensure the tool path considers previously machined areas, which is necessary for small holes that have already been drilled.
- Feed Rate Calculation: The feed rate for this operation is calculated using the diameter of the tool, which is 0.375 inches, and a radial stock of 0.1 inch. The resulting feed rate is set to 16,000 rpm at 15 inches per minute.
- Tool Path Selection: The tool path selected for this operation is designed to ensure the machine does not lose position, which is crucial for maintaining accuracy.
- Adjust Feed Rate for Small Holes: When working with small holes, slightly increase the feed rate. The speaker suggests starting at 16,000 rpm and 8.5 inches per minute as a conservative setting to avoid machine position loss.
- Chip Thinning Effect in Small Holes: As the radius of the hole gets closer to the tool's radius, chip thinning decreases, and at some point, there may be no chips. This requires slowing down the feed rate.
- Reduce Radius for Lower Speeds: If you decrease the velocity, you can use much tighter radiuses. For example, reducing speed from 30 to 10 inches per minute allows using a 23-inch bleed out radius.
- Adjust Plunge Feed Rate for Smooth Transitions: Slowing down the plunge feed rate to 30 inches per minute ensures smoother transitions and prevents excessive material removal issues.
- Deceleration Rate for Smooth Transitions: When transitioning from a plunge speed of about thirty inches per minute to eight and a half inches per minute, decelerate smoothly to avoid rapid changes.
- Model Offset for Countersinks: Set the top offset to 50 thousands and bottom offset to model bottom negative 30 to account for countersinks in some holes.
- Adaptive Pitch Adjustment: Adjust the pitch to about ten degrees for better fit, using an eyeball method rather than complex calculations.
- Avoiding Centripetal Acceleration Issues: Determine the feed rate manually to avoid centripetal acceleration problems before starting toolpaths.
- Speed Setting for Machining: The operator mentions setting the speed to 16,000 RPM and feed rate to 48 inches per minute.
- Feed Rate Adjustment for Small Holes: The operator adjusts the feed rate to 15,000 IPM and pitch to 48 for machining small holes.
- Tool Path Adjustment for Hole Accuracy: The operator mentions the importance of ensuring that holes are in the right place rather than being perfectly circular.
- Rest Machining for Roughing Tool Path: The operator sets up rest machining for the roughing tool path, offsetting it from previous operations.
- Handling Oversize Finishing in Roughing: The operator notes that the roughing tool path sometimes struggles with oversizing holes, suggesting a need to adjust settings accordingly.
- Lead In/Out Radius Setting: The lead in and out radius was set to 275, which is important for ensuring the toolpath does not cause issues with part spacing.
- Toolpath Generation Time: The toolpath generation took a long time due to the small tolerance and Rose officiating being on, making the model more accurate but increasing computation time.
- Scallop Toolpaths and Step Over: Using a narrow step over in scallop toolpaths can cause the tool to separate slightly, requiring multiple passes and potentially increasing processing time.
- Lead-in and Lead-out Radius: The lead-in and lead-out radius is set to seventy-five to avoid higher accelerations and forces, which can cause the machine to lose accuracy. A smaller radius would result in triple the force for surgical accelerations.
- Tool Bus Selection: Select the first tool bus and hold shift to select the last one, then right-click protect to organize everything into camp patterns and folders.
- Offset Tool Diameter Calculation: The offset tool diameter is calculated as the tool diameter times two plus ten, which was found to work well.
- Projection for Offsetting Part Edge: To offset the part edge, project the top face first by pressing the top face and then offset the purple dots in a 2D sketch.
- Avoid Overlapping Geometries in Toolpaths: When creating toolpaths, ensure there are no overlapping geometries to prevent the machine from getting confused and losing positional accuracy.
- Use Simpler Machining Methods for Complex Parts: For complex parts with overlapping features, simpler machining methods like those shown by Team C64 can be more effective and reduce machine movement.
- Adjust Tolerance and Stock to Leave for Faster Toolpaths: To generate faster toolpaths, adjust the tolerance and turn off stock to leave in the passes settings.
- Avoid Material Overcut: It's important for the software to know not to overcut material between parts.
- Toolpath Selection and Adjustment: When toolpaths are not sharing out correctly, you may need to select and adjust the tool path manually.
- Regenerate Toolpaths When Necessary: If there are issues with toolpaths, you may need to regenerate them.
- Use CAM Patterns for Efficiency: Using CAM patterns can help in setting up toolpaths efficiently, such as selecting direction and spacing.
- Pattern Creation Strategy: Do everything on one side of the part first, then move to the second side. Prioritize important features like holes before less critical ones.
- Edge Spacing Recommendation: Use an edge spacing of six pitches for tool paths.
- Machine Time Efficiency: Completing the machining process in 50 minutes is efficient compared to other teams that take up to two hours.
- Tool Path Depth and Chip Load: Using a full depth of quarter-inch with a chip load of five-and-a-half is effective for the machine scale.
- Trochoidal Toolpath Advantage: Using a trochoidal toolpath is gentler on the machine compared to other methods like three six four one.

tips.title: Fixturing & Workholding: CNC Vises & 2,4,6 Blocks
tips.text:
- CNC Vise Profile: A CNC vise has flat and ground sides, allowing you to rotate the vise up on its side or use precision flat edges for tramming.
- CNC Vise Jaw Movement: The movable jaw in a CNC vise is prone to jaw lift due to clearance for movement, but this is mitigated by two inclined planes that provide both forward and downward clamping force.
- Jaws in CNC Vises: CNC vise jaws are smooth to avoid marring parts, yet they offer incredible workholding power through high clamping force.
- Clamping Force vs Clamping Pressure: Clamping force is the consistent amount of torque applied to a screw, pushing forward with a fixed amount of force. Clamping pressure is how that force is distributed across the surface area of your part.
- Using Talon Johns for Minimal Material Holding: Talon Johns allow you to clamp with a relatively thin amount of material in the vise jaws without compromising work holding by distributing force across a smaller surface area.
- Extrusion Stress in Aluminum Parts: Most aluminum parts are extrusions, which can have some tension or stress along the x-axis. This can cause parts to curve or bow when flipped over using traditional vise jaws.
- Solving Bowing in Extruded Aluminum Parts: Ways to solve bowing in extruded aluminum parts include de-stressing the material, either in its billet form or after an initial operation, and removing equal amounts of material on both sides of the part.
- Flex Re-clamping for Stress-Free Machining: Leave as much material as possible to accommodate flex re-clamping in a stress-free state and re-deck the material again.
- Using Super Glue for Decking Off Top Hat: Used super glue technique to deck off the top hat in a CNC vise.
- Handling Curved Parts in CNC Vise: Used a traditional hard jaw CNC vise and an angle jig to hold a curved part at a specific angle for machining.
- Using Parallels for High-Up Machining: Held material relatively high up in a Tormach five-inch vise with parallels for machining.
- Using Custom Fixture and Angle Jig: Used a vice plus a custom fixture and an angle jig to hold the part at the right location for machining.
- Sandwiching Parts with 246 Blocks: Used two four six blocks to sandwich the part and increase clamping power of the vice.
- Using Threaded Rod and Backstop with 246 Blocks: Used a threaded rod and backstop made from pieces of steel through 246 blocks to hold a casting at an angle.
- Using Vises and 246 Blocks: Holding parts in a vise allows intentional spacing off or above the top of 246 blocks, enabling the use of a woodruff key for undercut relief.
- Single Setup with Vises and Blocks: Using a vise and 246 blocks allows machining operations to be done in one setup instead of two.
- Stabilizing Parts with Toe Jacks: A simple toe jack can be used to preload the tip of a part, adding stability and reducing chatter.
- Better Stability with Additional Blocks: Adding a second 246 block with a jack screw can sandwich the part, increasing preload and stability.
- Floating Studs for Consistent Clamping: Using studs to keep 246 blocks upright but allowing them to float, then squeezing with an F-style clamp can provide consistent clamping force.
- Consistent Clamping with Torque Wrench: Using a torque wrench to apply consistent clamping force ensures long-term process reliability and accurate parts.

tips.title: Custom Fixtures: Creative Workholding Strategies for CNC Machining!
tips.text:
- Custom Fixture for Carta Knife Handles: A custom fixture was necessary for the second operation on these carta knife handles. It proved to be a great workflow whether making two or 200 parts, with high process reliability and the ability to tweak as needed.
- Using Vise Edge Clamps for Thin Parts: Vise edge clamps were used to hold down the raw material for op1, allowing holes to be drilled and then screw-clamped to the fixture below for profile work.
- Vacuum Work Holding Plate and Mighty Bite Clamps for Casting Pattern: A vacuum work holding plate was used initially, followed by a combination of alignment blocks, mighty bite eccentric hex clamps, shims, and a saunders machine works fixture plate for the final operation.
- Custom Fixture with Mighty Bite Hex Clamps for Extrusion: A custom fixture using mighty bite hex clamps along the interior diameter and machine spacer blocks was built to hold an extrusion part, combined with existing screw holes and fasteners.
- Custom Fixture for Connecting Rods: Alex built a fixture that allowed machining multiple connecting rods in one setup, focusing on op 2 of the V8 engine project.
- Fixture for Giant Razor Blades: Designed and machined a fixture with pivoting straps to hold giant razor blades for machining bevels, including a datum for probing.
- Datum for Accurate Location: Used a laser-cut jig as a datum to accurately locate parts in the vice for machining operations.
- Consolidating Operations with Chamfering: Chamfering is a key to consolidating operations and reducing setups in custom fixturing.
- Custom Fixture for KTM Motorcycle Bracket: Designed a fixture plate that drops into a traditional six-inch vise to machine a KTM motorcycle bracket, including information for process reliability.

tips.title: GibbsCAM Tech Tip: How to Create a Trochoidal Toolpath
tips.text:
- Depth Matters in Dummy Operation: In the dummy operation, depth is crucial and should be taken directly off the part with no lead-in or lead-out.
- Stepover for Trochoidal Toolpath: The stepover for the trochoidal toolpath is set to 09, which is 6% of the 1/8 inch cutter.
- Tool Selection for Trochoidal Cut: A 1/8 inch solid carbide end mill is used for the trochoidal cut with an RPM of 14,500 and a feed rate of 14.7.

tips.title: CNC Basics - Everything a Beginner Needs To Know
tips.text:
- End Mills Purpose: End mills are purpose-built tools for CNC machines, designed with specific cutting edge geometry to cut materials efficiently.
- Tool Path Construction: In CNC milling, you manually create tool paths using software to instruct the machine on how fast to spin the spindle and move in specific directions.
- Work Holding Importance: Mounting material onto the machine, known as work holding, is crucial before running a CNC job.
- Design Considerations for CNC: CNC design differs from 3D printing as the cutter moves straight down, limiting features like overhangs unless using multi-axis machines.
- Feeds and Speeds Importance: For CNC machines, you need to specify how fast the tool spins and moves, known as feeds and speeds.
- CAM Software Usage: CAM software helps in creating tool paths for CNC machines, and different software like Fusion 360 and SolidWorks offer varying levels of automation.
- Tool Selection Strategy: Use multiple tools for different stages of CNC machining, starting with larger tools to remove most material before using smaller tools for finer details.
- Clamp System Caution: When securing material in a CNC router, be extremely careful with clamp systems as the cutting head can hit them. Use workarounds like wooden screws or double-sided super glue rigs to avoid issues.
- Double-Sided Super Glue Rig: A tip from nyccnc: Use double-sided super glue or wooden screws to secure material in a CNC router, so that if the cutting tool hits it, there's no damage.
- Tool Length Measurement: The CNC machine has no idea about the length of the tool, so you must tell it. This can be done manually by typing in an accurate measurement or automatically using a touch plate probe.
- Tool Change Procedure: When changing tools during a job, you need to measure and input the length of the new tool into the machine to avoid crashes.
- Fixturing for Repetitive Jobs: Fixturing is a type of work holding used to repeat a process without setting up from scratch each time, saving time and ensuring consistency.
- Sanding Wood After Machining: When working with wood, sanding is necessary to remove marks left by the tool.
- Chiseling Rounded Pockets in Wood: For traditional woodworking, rounded inside pockets may require chiseling to clean them out.
- Deburring Metal Parts After Milling: When milling metal, deburring is necessary to remove sharp edges from cut parts.
- Post-Machining Finishing Options: After CNC machining, additional finishing like sandblasting or polishing may be needed for a complete finish.

tips.title: How to Square and Indicate a Vise on Your CNC Mill – Haas Automation Tip of the Day
tips.text:
- Cleaning T-Slots Before Stoning: Clean T-slots with a brush and T-slot tool before stoning to remove chips.
- Using Fine Side of Stone for Vise Setup: Use the fine side of a stone, like silicon carbide or oil-filled aluminum oxide, to check for burrs and dents.
- Cleaning Table Before Stoning: Clean the table with a solvent or alcohol before stoning to prevent gunk from loading up the stone.
- Using Single Bolt for Vise Squaring: Use only one bolt to square the vise, allowing it to rotate around a pivot point when tapping with a mallet.
- Checking Vise Clearance Before Tightening: Check for clearance between the vise and machine components, such as doors and way covers, before fully tightening.
- Using Dead Blow Hammer for Vise Indicating: Use a dead blow hammer with lead shot and a soft face to tap the vise during indicating to avoid damage.

tips.title: Surface Roughness in Manufacturing: Must-Know Basics
tips.text:
- Surface Roughness Measurement Methods: Surface roughness can be measured using contact methods, which use a stylus to record height variations, or non-contact methods like laser scanning and optical interferometry that analyze the surface without physical contact.
- Roughness Average (RA) Parameter: Roughness Average (RA) is the most common parameter, representing the average height of surface irregularities over a given distance. Lower RA values indicate smoother surfaces.
- Surface Roughness in Manufacturing Processes: Different manufacturing processes have typical surface roughness ranges: milling (8 to 3.2 micrometers), turning (1.6 to 3.2 micrometers), grinding (0.2 micrometers), EDM (1.6 to 6.3 micrometers).
- Sharp Tools for Smoother Finish: A sharp, well-maintained tool will give you a smoother finish, while a worn out tool can leave a rough, uneven surface.
- Cutting Parameters Influence Surface Finish: Higher cutting speeds usually result in a finer finish, while slower speeds can leave more visible tool marks.
- Material Affects Surface Roughness: Softer materials like aluminum are easier to machine smoothly, while harder materials like stainless steel often end up with a rougher surface after machining.
- Surface Roughness Impact on Performance: Smoother surfaces can boost performance in many ways, like reducing friction and wear, but they often come with a higher price tag.
- Application-Specific Surface Finish Requirements: Precision bearings, aerospace components, and medical implants require ultra smooth surfaces for specific reasons like reducing friction and ensuring hygiene.

tips.title: How to Stop Chatter on CNC Milling Machine
tips.text:
- Chatter is a Misnomer: Chatter refers to when a tool or workpiece vibrates enough to cause surface problems.
- Interconnected Setup Aspects: Chatter solutions involve balancing work holding, tooling, and part program.
- Work Holding Importance: Proper work holding is crucial to prevent chatter, especially with long tools.
- Improving Work Holding: Use larger vices, center material, and wider jaws to improve work holding.
- Tooling Length Considerations: Shorten tool holders and flute lengths to dampen vibration.
- Use Short Flute Length Tools: Go with the shortest flute length possible for solid carbide tools, using only the flutes necessary for the pocket you need to create.
- Variable Flute Spacing Reduces Chatter: Tools with variable flute spacing can interrupt the cut and reduce chatter.
- Variable Helix and Pitch Teeth Help: Using tools with a variable helix and pitch teeth can also help in reducing chatter.
- Strengthen Workholding for Long Holders: If you have to use a long holder or end mill, strengthen your work holding or program.
- Adjust Tooling Frequency to Avoid Resonance: Changing the tooling slightly can adjust its natural frequency and stop chatter, similar to adjusting a tuning fork.
- Use Spindle Override to Adjust Speeds: The spindle override button is a useful tool for adjusting speeds and potentially stopping chatter.
- Adjusting RPM to Stop Chatter: Lowering the spindle speed (RPM) can often stop chatter, but for longer tools, increasing RPM might be necessary to get out of the resonance area.
- Tool Engagement and Chatter: Chatter can occur due to varying tool engagement percentages in different parts of a pocket or slot, requiring adjustments in RPM for each section.
- Constant Tool Engagement with Adaptive Tool Path: Using adaptive or dynamic tool paths ensures constant tool engagement, which helps in maintaining a consistent RPM and feed rate throughout the entire machining process.

tips.title: Plunge Milling Explained: Increase MRR & Eliminate Chatter with Axial Roughing
tips.text:
- Plunge Milling Strength in Z Axis: Your machine is strongest in the Z axis, making plunge milling effective for deep pockets, long overhangs, and tough materials due to its stability and reduced tool deflection.
- Indexable Plunge Mills Design: Indexable plunge mills have strong insert pockets, small or zero degree angles, and inserts designed for straight down cutting.
- Benefits of Plunge Roughing: Plunge roughing offers very high metal removal rates and easy cost control, with the ability to chip an insert, rotate it, and continue cutting.
- When to Use Plunge Milling: Use plunge milling when side milling chatters, you need long reach for deep features or tough materials like stainless steel, titanium, or super alloys.
- Tool Path Strategy for Plunge Milling: Plunge milling requires vertical plunges, limited radial engagement, and consistent step over to avoid extra work and worse results.
- Plunge Depth Control: If you're plunging more than three times D, split the plunge depth to maintain consistent engagement and protect inserts from recutting chips.
- Step Over Control: Smaller step over equals lighter load but more plunges, while larger step over provides higher load and faster roughing.
- Chip Evacuation in Plunge Milling: Plunge milling drops chips straight down, so program with radial retracts between plunges for better chip evacuation.
- Chip Packing Issues: Chip packing kills chips to clear and plunge tools faster than bad feeds.
- Feeds and Speeds Importance: Feeds and speeds matter in plunge milling.
- Load Requirement for Plunge Mills: Plunge mills need load, not milling or sympathy.
- Avoid Creeping Inserts: Don't creep; rubbing inserts cutting destroys edges.
- Axial vs Radial Load: Axial load is good; radial load is bad.
- Plunge Milling Suitability: Plunge milling is ideal for removing a ton of material.
- Respecting Physics in Plunge Milling: Plunge milling is about respecting physics.
- Roughing Strategy Caution: If your roughing strategy feels like daring the machine to fail, you're probably side milling something you should be plunge milling.

tips.title: Fusion 360 CAM - How to use the remaining stock from the previous setup
tips.text:
- Reusing Stock from Previous Setup: To reuse stock from a previous setup in Fusion 360 CAM, ensure that the model is a component and not just a body. Copy and rotate the component for the second operation instead of rotating the body within the component.
- Selecting Component vs Body in Setup: In the manufacturing workspace, select the component rather than the body when setting up your model for machining.
- Using F8 to Control Stock Visibility: Use the F8 shortcut in Fusion 360 CAM to control the visibility of in-process stock.
- Choosing Stock from Preceding Setup: When creating a second setup, choose the stock from the preceding setup and turn on 'Continue Rest Machining' to ensure the stock is in the correct position.
- Synchronized Active Setup: Use the 'Synchronized Active Setup' feature to control the visibility of components and fixtures relative to the current setup.

tips.title: 'Zero Tolerance Machining' with the Wire EDM, Making a Puzzle Cube - Part 2 | US Digital
tips.text:
- Brass Wire Thickness: The brass wire used in the EDM is typically 10,000 of an inch thick (about three times the size of a human hair) or sometimes 4,000 of an inch thick.
- Deionized Water in EDM: The EDM tank is filled with deionized water to ensure zero electrical current, making it safe to touch and allowing the camera lens to be placed underwater.
- Tolerance for EDM Projects: The typical tolerance for a project like this is 1/10th of a thousand of an inch.
- Wire Re-threading in EDM: After one piece comes out, the wire is re-threaded to cut the next piece.

tips.title: The Different Surface Finishes for CNC Machining (compared)
tips.text:
- As-Machined Finish Rule of Thumb: Use the as-machined finish for parts with tight tolerances where aesthetics are not an issue.
- Smooth Machining Rule of Thumb: Smooth machining is best for precise parts where the surface roughness needs to be fine, but it's not suitable for customer-facing products.
- Bead Blasting Rule of Thumb: Use bead blasting for parts with a matte uniform finish when dimensional tolerances are not a key concern.
- Brushing Rule of Thumb: Brushing is great for parts with long flat surfaces as it's easy to access with sandpaper.
- Anodizing Type 2 for Smooth Surface: Use anodizing type two to add a thin, aesthetically pleasing protective layer to your aluminium and titanium parts.
- Anodizing Type 3 for High Wear Resistance: Use anodizing type three in engineering applications where very high wear resistance and surface hardness are required.
- Powder Coating for High Impact Strength: Use powder coating for applications where high impact strength is required or to finish parts that cannot be anodized.

tips.title: Fusion 360 2D adaptive, High Speed Machining (HSM) AKA Trochoidal Milling Explained
tips.text:
- Use Climb Cutting for Smaller Tools: For smaller tools, it's recommended to only use climb cutting to avoid snapping the end mill.
- Set Optimum Load for Chip Control: The optimum load is set to 20 percent of the end mill's diameter, which in this case is 70 thousandths.
- Avoid Roughing Both Ways with Small Tools: Roughing both ways (climb and conventional) can cause the end mill to snap, especially with smaller tools.
- Set Minimum Cutting Radius: The minimum cutting radius is set to 10 percent of the tool diameter.
- Depth of Cut Recommendation: Typically use about three times the diameter of the end mill for depth of cut. If five times the diameter, consider multiple depths.
- Smoothing in Fusion 360: Turn smoothing on to avoid beating the machine to death, especially without high-speed look ahead.
- High-Speed Machining Mode: Use high-speed machining mode with a feed rate of up to 500 inches per minute.
- Minimum Stay Down Distance: Set the minimum stay down distance to 1 and 7/8 inches (78 thousands) for optimal end mill usage.
- Chip Load and Lift Height: Ensure chip load is lower than lift height to avoid dragging chips across the surface or picking them up.
- Helix Entry for Inside Cuts: Use helix entry for inside cuts to avoid issues with the tool path.
- Adaptive Milling Helical Diameter Calculation: If your total diameter is 375, the helical diameter would be tool diameter plus 90 percent.
- Minimizing Helical Entry Time: Starting the helical entry below the surface of the part by 0.3 or 0.5 inches can save significant machine time.
- Control Over Adaptive Milling Pockets: By duplicating and editing the adaptive process, you can have full control over each pocket in your program.
- Machine Time is Money: Efficient use of machine time by minimizing unnecessary operations can lead to more billable hours and cost-effective parts.

tips.title: Trochoidal Milling Machining - Iscar Plus
tips.text:
- High-Speed Trochoidal Milling Strategy: Trochoidal milling is a high-speed machining strategy where the tool moves in a circular path with continuous forward motion, reducing heat buildup and forces, which helps with chip evacuation and reduces vibration.
- E7 Tool for Trochoidal Milling: The E7 tool from Iscar is ideal for trochoidal milling due to its extra long flute length, chip splitters, and thick core.
- Benefits of Rigid Holder and Machine in Trochoidal Milling: Using a rigid holder and machine in trochoidal milling reduces vibration, improves surface finish, enhances predictability, and is easier on the tool and machine.

tips.title: Tips for 3D Finishing of Sloped Part Surfaces with a Ball Nose Cutter
tips.text:
- Ball Nose Cutter for Sloped Surfaces: Use a ball nose cutter for sloped surfaces to handle peaks and valleys better than other cutters.
- 45 Degree Tool Path for Slopes: Run a 45-degree tool path rather than a zero or 90-degree angle to provide a smoother transition and better surface finish.

tips.title: Milling machine tutorial - cutter selection, speeds and feeds, coolant, high speed machining
tips.text:
- Use Largest Diameter Cutter Possible: When selecting a cutter, use the largest diameter that will produce the correct geometry without exceeding the dimensions of the part features.
- Consider Cutter Diameter for Radius Features: Ensure the cutter diameter does not exceed the radius of inside features to avoid incorrect geometry.
- Small Diameter Cutters for Tight Corners: Use small diameter cutters for tight internal corners, but be aware they are more prone to breaking.
- Avoid Small Internal Radius Cuts: Small internal radius cuts are challenging and can lead to broken cutters; aim for the closest achievable radius.
- Choose Appropriate Cutter Length: Select a cutter that is not unnecessarily long for the depth of the feature being machined.
- Short Cutter Length for Stability: Using a short cutter is crucial to maintain rigidity in your setup, especially for shallow pockets. A long cutter can wobble too much, leading to poor finish quality.
- High-Speed Steel for Hobbyists: For hobbyists, high-speed steel tooling is sufficient and allows you to work at a reasonable speed without the need for carbide tooling.
- Coatings May Not Be Necessary for Soft Materials: In the context of cutting aluminum and plastics, coatings like titanium nitride may not be beneficial and a sharp tool is generally preferred.
- High-Speed Steel for Aluminum and Plastic: High-speed steel uncoated tools are perfectly fine for milling aluminum and plastic, as they are cheaper than carbide.
- Carbide Tool Brittleness: Carbide tools are more brittle and may chip if the setup is wobbly.
- Spindle Speed Determined by Material: The spindle speed depends on the material of the cutter and workpiece, determined empirically from speeds and feeds charts.
- Cutting Edge Pressure: The cutting pressure developed at the edge is extremely high due to the small contact area, independent of cooling methods.
- High-Speed Cutting Risk: Pushing a high-speed cutter too fast can cause the edge to fall apart due to excessive temperature and pressure.
- Tungsten Carbide Tooling: Using tungsten carbide tooling, which is a composite of tungsten carbide particles bound in a cobalt matrix, can improve durability and performance.
- Tool Material Limitation: The material of the tool is typically the limiting factor in machining operations, not the power of the machine.
- High-Speed Steel Speed Range for Aluminum: For high-speed steel cutters on aluminum alloys like 6061, a good surface feet per minute (SFM) range is between 450 and 650.
- RPM Calculation Approximation: Machinists often approximate RPM using the formula: RPM = SFM * 4 / tool diameter, since Pi is close to 3.
- RPM Adjustment for Machine Limit: The RPM is set to 3,800 as it's a good comfortable speed for the machine and it's okay to go slower. It can't exceed the top speed of the milling machine.
- Speed Limit Based on Material: The maximum surface feet per minute is a limit on how fast you can spin the tool in aluminum without breaking it down prematurely. Plastic allows for higher speeds due to less cutting force.
- Chip Load for Slot Cutting: For a slot with a 38-inch tool diameter in aluminum, the chip load is 0.0038 inches per tooth, which describes how much material is removed per tooth on the cutter.
- Tool Breakage Risk: Going too fast in the linear direction can cause the tool to break, regardless of how quickly you're spinning it.
- Avoid Overloading the Tool: Spinning the tool too quickly can cause it to snap off or dull. It's better not to go slower than the recommended RPM, as going too slow can lead to burnishing and premature cutter wear.
- Chip Load Importance: Not taking a big enough chip can cause the material to burnish instead of cut, dulling the cutter quickly. It's important to follow the manufacturer's recommendation for chip load.
- Flute Count and Feed Rate: When cutting slots, a two-flute end mill is preferable as it allows chips to escape more easily. However, using a four-flute end mill can double the feed rate for deep pockets.
- Chip Clearance Importance: It is crucial to have chip clearance to get chips out, especially in deep pockets.
- Cutter Approach Method: Some cutters cannot go straight down into material and need to approach from the side, angle, or helix.
- Plunge Depth Rule of Thumb: A good rule of thumb is not to plunge more than half the diameter of the cutter into material per cut.
- Roughing and Finishing Cuts: For almost all machining operations, do roughing cuts first to get a little bit under size, then perform finishing cuts for final dimension and surface finish.
- Minimize Cutting Load for Better Finish: The last cut should only remove a small amount of material (5 or 10 thousandths of an inch) to reduce cutting load, deflection, and achieve better finish and accuracy.
- Coolant Benefits for Aluminum: Aluminum benefits from coolant (mist or flood) to prevent chips from sticking and transferring heat back into the workpiece, avoiding global heating issues.
- Adjust Speed and Feed Without Coolant: Without coolant, reduce cutting speed and adjust feed rate to maintain constant chip load to prevent overheating.
- Climb Milling on Older Machines: On older milling machines, climb milling (cutting into the rotation) may not work well due to free play and mechanics causing chatter.
- Conventional vs Climb Milling: In conventional milling, the chip starts small and gets thicker as it comes out. In climb milling, the chip starts thick and becomes thin. Modern machines use climb milling for better surface finish.
- Chip Load Rule of Thumb: A good rule of thumb is to divide the diameter of the cutter by 150 to get a conservative chip load for small endmills.
- Cutter Diameter Selection: Use the biggest cutter diameter that you comfortably can, generally not larger than 3/4 of an inch for small machines.
- High-Speed Machining Philosophy: In high-speed machining, spin the tool as fast as your machine can handle, especially with carbide tooling and non-ferrous materials.
- Coolant Usage in High-Speed Machining: Use lots of cooling when performing high-speed machining to maximize tool life and performance.
- High-Speed Machining Deep Plunge Technique: In high-speed machining, use a very deep plunge but do not go too far in the width of your cut. This technique allows using more of the cutter depth and removing material quickly.
- Rigidity is Key in Machining: Rigidity of the setup is more important than the coating of your bit or the number of flutes. Use the shortest and largest diameter cutter possible, and clamp work securely.
- Material Removal Efficiency: High-speed machining emphasizes using as much of the cutter depth as possible and taking off material laterally within machine capacity to remove material quickly.
- Quinch Cutter Flexibility: Using a quinch cutter or bigger provides more flexibility for your machine, especially if it wobbles slightly. With smaller cutters, there are fewer second chances, and they can be ruined easily in materials like aluminum.

tips.title: High Speed Machining Toolpaths Changing American Manufacturing
tips.text:
- High Speed Machining on Low Power Machines: Volume L toolpaths can transform a low-power machine (10,000 rpm spindle) into a high-speed milling machine by cutting 6061-T6 aluminum at 350 inches per minute, reducing cycle time by more than 60%.
- High Speed Machining on Hard Steel: Volume L toolpaths allow machining centers to safely cut 4140 steel at 1,300 surface feet per minute, which is four times faster than the manufacturer's recommended rate, reducing cycle time by nearly 70%.
- High Speed Machining on Titanium: A carbide end mill can make a full one-inch deep cut at 126 inches per minute in 6Al-4V titanium, nearly four times the recommended feed rate without an air blast, reducing cycle time by more than 70% and doubling tool life.

tips.title: How to Set Up a 5 Axis CNC Machine | DVF 5000 | DN Solutions
tips.text:
- Even Pressure on Stone: When using a stone, maintain even pressure across the table surface to avoid any burrs or catches.
- Check for Burrs and Catches: While using a stone, check for any burrs or catches that might indicate an uneven surface.
- Clean Table with Towel: Use a clean towel to wipe the table after stoning, focusing on small sections at a time to remove all grit.
- Follow Setup Sheet for Vice Selection: Refer to the setup sheet to determine the correct vice and riser to use, as specified by the programmer.
- Documentation Importance: Good documentation is Paramount and key to success in five axis Machining.
- Vice Setup on Riser: The vice is mounted on the Riser as specified on the setup sheet.
- Clean Bottom of Vice: Make sure the bottom is clean before setting it on the table.
- Tilted Work Plane or Dynamic Fixture Offsets: Use tilted work plane or dynamic fixture offsets to place the vice and work offset wherever you want on the table.
- Avoid Theoretical Center Line Programming: Programming from the theoretical center line of the machine is outdated and requires precise alignment.
- Check CAM Software Output: Ensure your cam software outputs tilted work plane or dynamic fixture offsets.
- Five Axis Tightening Advantage: In five axis machining, you can adjust bolts to line them up without knocking anything around.
- Eccentric Tool Measurement: When installing an eccentric tool, measure the length roughly with calipers before touching off on the machine.
- Tool Length Input for Eccentric Tools: For eccentric tools, input a rough length measurement before touching off to get an accurate tool offset.
- On-Center Tool Setup: For on-center tools, you don't need to know the exact length; just input the tool number for setup.
- Tool Number Input: Input the tool number correctly to ensure the machine uses the right tool.
- Tool Measurement Verification: Verify the measured length of tools to ensure accuracy in machining.
- Tool Wear Check: Check for any wear on tools to prevent machining issues.
- Quick Vice Indication Method: Use the center pivot point to quickly zero and measure the vice on a 5-axis machine.
- Ensure Fixture is Flat: The vice or fixture must be flat with the table. If not, adjust it by shimming to ensure it is level.
- Do Not Set a Number in B Axis Offset: Avoid entering a number in the B axis offset as it will cause incorrect calculations.
- Clamp Material in Center of Vice: Clamp the part in the center of the vice using the serrated teeth at 3 mm deep and torque to 50 ft-lb.
- Set Vise Stop Appropriately: Install a vise stop on the left side of the vice, ensuring it does not stick out too far above the jaws to avoid hitting it during machining.
- Material Clearance Above Vice: Ensure the material sticks out above the top of the vice by at least 2.88 mm.
- Setting Z Offset Correctly: Ensure that the Z offset is set to -20,000 from the top of the stock as per the setup sheet.
- Probing on Raw Stock: It is not a good thing to probe on raw stock when holding a finished part. Reprobe on the finished size after excess stock is removed.

tips.title: Top Tips to Get the Perfect Fixture | Fixture Friday 3 | Pierson Workholding
tips.text:
- Start Small with Pallet Design: Encourage customers to start small and keep it simple when creating multi-operation pallets, focusing on one operation at a time.
- Slotting Parts for Efficiency: Slot apart every other part so that two parts come connected at the end of the cycle, allowing them to be placed in a machine with one work stop.
- Use Machined Edges for Touch Off: Create a machined edge in the corner of the pallet as an optional touch off point to verify setups more accurately.
- Use Pockets for Clamps with Helicoil Inserts: Create pockets instead of slots for clamps and install Helicoil thread inserts to extend the life of threads.

tips.title: Backlash Deflection and Vibration   Chapter 2
tips.text:
- Deflection and Backlash Impact on Accuracy: Deflection due to cutting load primarily affects accuracy in roughing passes, while backlash is more significant in finishing passes.
- Deflection and Cutting Speed Relationship: Deflection limits the cutting speed by allowing vibrations to develop, which can build a positive feedback loop increasing vibration amplitude.
- Impact of Vibrations and Resonances: Vibrations and resonances can lead to poor finish, broken cutters, damaged workpieces, or even damage to parts of the machine.
- Understanding Backlash: Backlash is lost movement in the linear motion system where we request a change in direction. It can be visualized as carrying a bowling ball in a box; each time we reverse direction, we have to move the box far enough for the ball to hit the opposite wall before it follows.
- Understanding Slack: Slack is very similar to backlash but occurs not due to the drive belts, but simply through slack in the mechanism such as the v-wheels which allow movements not controllable by the motors and belts.
- Understanding Deflection: Deflection is where the machine moves from the requested position due to forces encountered while cutting or by the operator. It can cause cutter engagement to be larger or smaller than intended, affecting the cutting load and causing vibration.
- Deflection Causing Vibration: Deflection can cause the machine to vibrate and resonate with the deflection of the cutting loads, which is a major limit to cutting speed on light machines like the Shopoko.
- Vibration Modes and Cutting Speed: Most users have experienced vibration modes when pushing their machine into heavier cuts where small vibrations can rapidly build up into large vibrations, which are then difficult to suppress.
- Tool Deflection Rule of Thumb: Keep tool deflection due to cutting forces below one thousandth of an inch to avoid chatter.
- Stability Load Diagrams: Plot stability load diagrams of your machine and tool combination to manage chatter.
- High Frequency Vibrations: High frequency vibrations occur in high speed spindles where small masses like cutters vibrate on very stiff springs.
- Low Frequency Vibrations: Lower frequency vibrations occur where heavy parts of the machine assembly vibrate against less stiff springs, such as the z carriage and spindle assembly.
- Deflection and Resonance in Cutting: Cutting forces cause deflection of the cutter and workpiece, leading to reduced engagement and increased cutting force as the machine springs back into the cut. This can create a positive feedback system that resonates if the frequency matches a resonance mode of the tool, workpiece, or machine.
- Resonance Modes and Energy Development: Resonance modes, especially with little damping, can develop a lot of energy once excited, continuing to feed themselves during the cut and causing variations in the cut surface.
- Frequency Range for Hobby Grade Machines: For hobby grade machines like Shapoko, vibrations triggered directly by cutter rotation at spindle speed are expected in the range of 200Hz to 2kHz. These frequencies are generally not visible to the naked eye.
- Lower Frequency Modes in Machines: In addition to spindle frequency vibration, lower frequency modes can build up in the machine as resonance, affecting elements like the Z carriage and spindle.
- Resonant Frequency Observation: An approximate resonant frequency of 22 hertz was observed, which is consistent with visible resonance modes on the machine.
- High V Wheel Pre-Tension Benefit: High v wheel pre-tension seems to help improve machine performance by reducing vibration.
- Mass Addition Impact on Resonance: Adding mass to the machine lowers resonant frequency but increases vibration amplitude when resonance occurs.
- Resonant Frequency Difference Between Machines: The standard size Shapoko 3 has a resonant frequency almost three times higher than the XXL model due to spring constant differences.
- Cutting Technique for Resonance Modes: To achieve maximum cutting rate, use a shallow but wide cut instead of a deep but thin cut to avoid excessive engagement and cutting force.
- Helix Angle Impact on Cutting Forces: Cutters with a high helix angle create significant vertical forces, especially in deep cuts, which can excite coupled deflection.
- Identify Major Deflection Sources: Identify large sources of deflection close to the cutter as major targets for reducing slack and improving rigidity.
- Reduce Slack and Improve Rigidity: To reduce slack and improve rigidity, focus on major deflection sources near the cutter.
- Increase Damping First: First, increase damping in the z-axis and spindle to address v-wheel radial deflection.
- Address V-Wheel Axial Deflection: Second, address v-wheel axial deflection affecting z-axis and spindle nodding.
- Handle Belt Tension Deflection: Third, handle z-axis and spindle translation left to right against belt tension.
- Consider Baseboard Deflection on XXL Machines: On XXL machines, consider the bouncy baseboard as a source of deflection.

tips.title: How to improve chip control in turning operations - Tips film #40
tips.text:
- Use Smaller Nose Radius: Using a smaller nose radius than usual can help with chip breaking and reduce long, stringy chips that cause jams.
- Select Tool with Precision Coolant: Consider selecting a tool with precision coolant paired with an insert geometry that offers better chip breaking capability to increase feed and depth of cut.
- Turn Towards Shoulder in Conventional Turning: To avoid chip jamming, turn towards the shoulder and stop before the dimension of the shoulder.
- Maintain Feed Rate for Horizontal Cuts: Maintain the same feed rate for four horizontal cuts in conventional turning.
- Final Vertical Cut Direction: The final vertical cut should be done from outer diameter towards the inner diameter in conventional turning.
- PrimeTurning Chip Control: PrimeTurning starts the cut at the chuck and removes material toward the end of the component, avoiding chip jamming with long, thin, and straight chips.
- PrimeTurning Feed Reduction: With PrimeTurning, always use feed reduction and a radial entry to maintain tolerances.
- Chip Evacuation Direction in PrimeTurning: In PrimeTurning, chips should break toward the unmachined surface to form a roll that breaks consistently.

tips.title: How Does Machining Affect A Metal's Surface Finish? - Mechanical Engineering Explained
tips.text:
- Effect of Tool Shape on Surface Roughness: The shape of the tool affects the texture and roughness created on the metal surface during machining.
- Influence of Cutting Speed on Surface Roughness: The speed at which the tool moves during machining influences the amount of surface roughness created.
- Material Removal Rate Impact on Surface Roughness: The amount of material removed at once during machining affects the surface roughness.
- Achieving Smoother Finish with Finer Tools and Slower Speeds: Using finer tools or slowing down the cutting speed can achieve a smoother finish with lower raw values.
- Initial Machining Sets Surface Finish Stage: The quality of the initial machining process sets the stage for the final surface finish.
- Balancing Machining Parameters for Optimal Surface Quality: Balancing the speed of machining, tool condition, and cutting tool design is key to optimizing surface quality.

tips.title: This KNOWLEDGE Will Ease Your Pain and Suffering When Attempting to Machine Perfect Parts
tips.text:
- Understanding Chatter: Chatter is a vibratory occurrence between the workpiece and cutting tool, causing a whining noise and wavy pattern on the part.
- Chatter Causes: Chatter occurs when machining parameters are not optimal, leading to the tool bouncing against the material.
- Testing Setup: Using three boring bars (steel and carbide) with different nose radius inserts to replicate real-world scenarios for reducing chatter.
- Engel's Techniques: Applying Engel's techniques to reduce chatter on a part with thin walls and ID turning.
- Avoid Chatter for 32 Surface Finish: To achieve a 32 surface finish, maintain a specific feed rate for each nose radius and keep the speed locked in while adjusting other parameters as necessary.
- Consistent Tool Length for Chatter Reduction: Use boring bars of the same length to eliminate variation in stick-out and reduce chatter.
- Adjust Speed for Chatter-Free Machining: Reduce speed near the back of parts that stick out far to minimize chatter, but aim for a consistent parameter that runs the part chatter-free from front to back.
- Use Appropriate Tooling for Surface Finish: Avoid using certain tool combinations like the 031 insert with this setup, as it results in poor surface finish and chatter.
- Adjust Speed for Chatter Reduction: When using a boring bar, start at half of the recommended speed to avoid chatter.
- Reduce Depth of Cut for Better Finish: Reducing depth of cut from 30 to 20 can improve surface finish.
- Nose Radius Impact on Chatter: Reducing nose radius from 31 to 156 drastically reduces chatter, improving surface finish.
- Consistent Surface Finish with Lower Nose Radius: Using a lower nose radius (156) results in a more consistent surface finish, though not ideal.
- Speed and Feed for Surface Finish: Running at 300 sfm with a feed rate of 1/4 inch per revolution can achieve a 32 surface finish.
- Tool Selection for Chatter Reduction: Using an 8-radius tool can reduce chatter and improve surface finish.
- Heavy Metal Bar as a Compromise: Using heavy metal bar can be a compromise between carbide and steel in terms of rigidity and cost.
- Nose Radius Impact on Surface Finish: Changing the nose radius from 70 to 156 resulted in a significant improvement in surface finish, dropping it from around 225 RA to just above 50 RA.
- Speed Adjustment for Chatter Reduction: Reducing the speed from a higher value to 300 SFM helped in reducing chatter and improving surface finish.
- Carbide Bar Choice: Using a carbide bar with a smaller nose radius (156) resulted in the best surface finish of 26 RA, showing that material choice and tool geometry are crucial.
- Reducing Surface Finish: By changing the boring bar material to a denser one, it reduced deflection and absorbed vibration, leading to a better surface finish from 25 RA to 22 RA.
- Impact of Nose Radius on Chatter: Using a smaller nose radius reduced cutting forces, which made the part less likely to chatter.

tips.title: Programming 5 Axis W/ Zero Experience | CNC Machining | Vlog #80
tips.text:
- Understanding CAM Process: During the CAM process, you need to tell the machine everything it needs to know so that when the code comes out, it will execute based on your instructions.
- Importance of Precision in CNC Machining: Putting the wrong decimal in the wrong place can crash the machine, highlighting the importance of precision.
- Sharing Knowledge in CNC Machining: A lot of people don't share information in the CNC machining trade, so everyone has to reinvent the wheel. The academy aims to change this by sharing knowledge throughout tutorials.
- Workholding in CNC Machining: The first operation involves holding the raw stock, flipping it face in a vise, and performing engraving with a corner round tool to put a radius on.
- Using Patterning for Circular Operations: You can use patterning to rotate an operation around a part in a circular pattern. This allows you to create multiple pockets or surfaces by defining one tool path and rotating it 360 degrees.
- Face Milling on a Flat Surface: When milling a flat surface, you can use a face mill and rotate the part with the 5-axis machine so that the cutting edge is perpendicular to the surface.
- Using Ball Mills for Radii: For milling radii, a ball mill is used to achieve the desired curvature.
- Understanding Part Design and Programming: It's important to understand the part design intimately before programming, as this knowledge helps in creating accurate tool paths and avoiding errors.
- Ensure Rigidity in Workholding: Make sure you have rigidity in the work holding and spindle to ensure stable machining.
- Follow Tutorials for Five Axis Machining: Nicole recommends following all the tutorials and prerequisite parts to understand the basic functions of a five-axis machine.
- Perfect Tool Paths and Checklists: Ensure your tool paths are perfect and go through checklists to avoid errors.
- Dry Run Your Setup: Nicole advises to dry run your setup to ensure everything is zeroed perfectly before running the actual part.
- Take Your Time: Nicole emphasizes the importance of taking your time to ensure everything is done correctly.

tips.title: Fusion 360 Flat Toolpath Strategy: Rest Machining Update | Autodesk Fusion 360
tips.text:
- Use Rest Machining for Efficiency: The flat strategy now supports rest machining, which removes only the material left over from previous toolpaths, saving time and avoiding unnecessary marking of the part.
- Specify a Smaller Tool for Rest Machining: To enable rest machining, specify a smaller tool than what was used in the previous operation to access areas left over by larger tools.
- Check Rest Machining Option in Geometry Tab: In the geometry tab, check the rest machining option to guide the flat strategy on what material remains to be machined.
- Detection Limit for Fragments: The detection limit can be increased to remove smaller fragments, taking the remaining stock into account.
- Rest Machining with Multiple Depths: When using multiple depths, the rest machining option only cuts where residual material exists, making it a smarter option for some 2D pockets.
- Progressively Reduce Tool Diameter with Rest Machining: Rest machining can be used to stack flat strategies where you progressively reduce the tool diameter or use it in conjunction with other strategies.

tips.title: Affordable Tool for Mirror Surface Finish! WW249
tips.text:
- Avoid Large Diameter Tools on Lower Power Machines: The operator recommends avoiding large diameter tools on lower power machines and suggests using quarter-inch tools when possible due to cost and pressure considerations.
- Depth to Diameter Ratio for Safety: The operator suggests a depth to diameter ratio of four times the tool diameter as a safe zone, meaning a quarter-inch tool should not exceed one inch in depth of cut.
- Tool Diameter and Chatter Issues: Running into problems like chatter, bad surface finish, bad tolerance, and deflection becomes more common when the tool diameter increases.
- Reflection and Surface Roughness: A reflective surface generally has a low roughness average (Ra) because light reflects back directly without big undulations or inconsistencies.
- Profilometer Usage: A profilometer measures the peaks and valleys on a surface to determine its roughness average (Ra). It's sensitive and requires careful calibration.
- Blanchard Grind vs Surface Grinder: A Blanchard grind typically has a different appearance compared to a surface grinder, even if both achieve similar roughness averages (Ra).
- Edge Grind and Margin Impact: The edge grind and margin of a cutting tool significantly affect surface finish, likely due to burnishing along the part.
- Uniformity in Multi-Flute Tools: For multi-flute tools, uniformity and consistency between all edges in the grind are crucial for achieving a mirror-like finish.
- Tolerance Changes Affect Surface Finish and Tool Pressure: Changes in tolerance affect surface finish, tool pressure, and deflection, impacting the final finish.
- Microscope for Surface Finish Inspection: Using a microscope, such as a $5 USB microscope with a scaled measuring unit, helps inspect surface finish and understand cutting action.
- Feed Per Tooth Calculation: The feed per tooth can be calculated and observed under a microscope to understand the physical nature of cutting action.
- Erratic Behavior Troubleshooting: Investigate erratic behavior just left of zero, which could be due to harmonic issues in the machine tool or holder.

tips.title: How Wire EDM Works
tips.text:
- Wire EDM Precision: Wire EDM can make precise cuts in metal with a blade no thicker than human hair, achieving microscopic particle removal and tight tolerances.
- Wire EDM Process Explanation: In wire EDM, a charged hair-thin wire removes microscopic particles from the workpiece using electrical sparks in deionized water.
- Deionized Water Role: Deionized water in wire EDM controls sparking, cools the process, and flushes away tiny particles.
- Particle Size in Wire EDM: The particles removed by wire EDM are about the size of a particle of smoke, typically 2 microns or smaller.
- Versatility of Wire EDM: Wire EDM can work with difficult materials, create complex shapes, and make very small parts.
- Small Hole EDM: There is a technique called small hole EDM for working from the inside of the hole to the outside.
- Automation in Wire EDM: Wire EDM is completely automated and CNC controlled, requiring no human involvement.

tips.title: How to Make Your Own Workholding on a Budget
tips.text:
- Repeatable Fixture Design: Design a two-piece fixture with a base plate and a top plate for repeatable setup. The base plate stays inside the machine with locating pins, while the top plate bolts to the part.
- Avoid Clamping on Finish Surfaces: To avoid damaging the finish, do not clamp directly onto surfaces that need to remain smooth.
- Use Lock Down Quick Change Kit: Utilize the lock down quick change kit from Mighty Bite for secure and repeatable clamping of fixtures.
- Locating Pins for Precision Alignment: Incorporate locating pins (round and diamond-shaped) into the fixture design to ensure precise alignment of parts.
- Press Fit Alignment: The turned-down section at the top of the bushings helps align press-fit pins perfectly.
- Knurled Bushing Installation: For knurled bushings without lead-in holes, a counterbore is added to help start the installation.
- Endmill for Flat Bottom Holes: After drilling holes, an endmill is used to mill a flat bottom at the bottom of the holes.
- Slot Design for Pin Retention: Slots and set screws are used to hold pins in place, preventing them from falling out during rotation.
- Repeatable Process Design: The design ensures a perfectly located and locked-in-place top plate, providing a repeatable process.
- Quick Fixture Setup with Bolts: Using a bolt through the bottom of the grid rip allows for quick setup and location without having to worry about indicating or probing every time.

tips.title: Feeds, speeds and depth of cut in 6061 aluminium alloy in a small cnc lathe. Trying for chip control
tips.text:
- Depth of Cut and Chip Control: Using a two mil deep cut at 0.05 feet per rev results in long continuous springs of swarf, which can cause damage to the surface finish.
- One Mil Cut and Chip Control: A one mil cut at 0.1 feet per rev results in broken chips, which are less problematic than long continuous springs but still cause mess.
- Very Shallow Cut and Chip Control: A very shallow cut with a 0.2 feed rate does not work well for chip breaking effect, resulting in long springs of swarf.
- Depth of Cut and Chip Control Experiment: A 1.34 depth of cut with a 0.08 feet per rev feed rate also results in breaking chips, but they can be difficult to find due to the mess.
- Surface Finish Issues: Long continuous springs of swarf can cause damage to the surface finish, especially when they get caught around the chuck and part.

tips.title: Comparing Tool Holders: Nut and Collet, Hydraulic Clamping, Thermogrip, and Hydraulic Press Fit.
tips.text:
- Standard Nut Collet Tool Holder Advantages: Low-cost, readily available, easy to change, adaptable to many shank sizes with different collets and cutouts.
- Standard Nut Collet Tool Holder Disadvantages: Lower gripping strength and run-out compared to other types.
