- Hydraulic Tool Holder Advantages: Vibration dampening, easy to change out tooling with no special equipment required, sleeves allow multiple shank sizes.
- Hydraulic Tool Holder Disadvantages: Gripping strength and run-out deteriorate with continued use.
- Thermo Grip or Shrink Fit Tool Holder Advantages: Low profile for tight spots, excellent gripping strength, very low run-out, great balance, faster speeds, better cut quality, longer tool life.
- Tool Holder Initial Cost: These tool holders require specialty equipment for heating and cooling, which increases the initial cost.
- Tool Holder Size Limitation: The holder fits one size shank only.
- High Grip Strength Requirement: This tool holder is recommended when high grip strength or phenolic machining and/or low run-out is required.
- Tool Holder for Small Diameter Tools: These tool holders are suitable for multi-flute tools and extremely small diameter tools.
- Improved Sidewall Finish: These tool holders can be used for obtaining better sidewall finish and getting into tight spots.
- Hydraulic Press Fit Tool Holder Advantages: Provides three micron run-out with high vibration dampening and the highest gripping strength in the market.
- Faster Feeds and Better Cut Quality: These tool holders equate to faster feeds, better cut quality, and longer tool life.
- Single Holder for Various Tool Diameters: You only need different Kaulitz holders for various tool diameters as they fit into this holder.
- Tool Holder Disadvantages: The initial cost and special equipment for changing the tool are disadvantages.

tips.title: Effects of Proper Cutter Engagement from Sandvik Coromant
tips.text:
- Chip Thinning Below 50% Engagement: When the milling cutter is engaged below 50%, chip thinning occurs and feed should be increased to maintain proper chip thickness.
- Programming Based on Center Line for Low Engagement: Cutters with low levels of engagement must be programmed based on the center line of the tool coming off the workpiece to maintain chip thickness.
- Entry Angle Impact on Chip Thinning: A chip thinning effect starts when the insert is turned onto a 45° angle, but it can be avoided with proper chip thickness and utilizing entry angles.
- Productivity Increase with Small Entry Angles: Small entry angles are ideal for high feed machining with low depths of cut, increasing productivity by up to 40% and allowing nearly six times the feed rate.
- Importance of Proper Chip Thickness: Maintaining proper chip thickness is crucial as inserts are designed to handle specific chip loads, and failing to do so can result in premature insert wear.

tips.title: Avoid Chatter on Your Mill - Haas Automation Tip of the Day
tips.text:
- Chatter Definition: Chatter is when a tool or workpiece vibrates enough to cause surface problems.
- Interconnected Setup Aspects: Workholding, tooling, and part program are interconnected; if one is compromised, the others need to compensate.
- Workholding Improvement: Improve workholding by using a larger vice, centering the material, and making wider jaws for better support.
- Tool Shortening to Reduce Chatter: Shorten tools, holders, and flute lengths to dampen vibration.
- Variable Flute Spacing and Helix: Use tools with variable flute spacing or helix to interrupt the cut and reduce chatter.
- Resonance Explanation: Chatter can be caused by resonance between tooling and workholding; adjusting RPMs or feeds/speeds can help.
- Adaptive Tool Path for Constant Engagement: Use adaptive tool paths to maintain constant tool engagement, reducing the need to adjust RPMs or feeds/speeds.

tips.title: TOP 5 tips to become a Master CNC Machine Programmer | DVF 5000 5 Axis Mill
tips.text:
- Keep an Open Mind: Always keep an open mind and be willing to learn new things, as there is always a better way to do something in machining.
- Avoid Distorting Parts with Vices: Holding parts in a vice too tightly can distort the part, leading to out-of-tolerance features. Use a balanced and appropriate clamping force.
- Listen to Peers' Advice: Always consider the advice of your peers, as they may have insights or experiences that you are overlooking.
- Understand All Variables in Machining: To determine the best machining method, understand variables like spindle connection, tool holder, fixturing, material properties, feeds, speeds, metal removal rates, and risk/reward.
- Adjust Speeds and Feeds for Extended Holders: When using extended length holders, adjust speeds and feeds to prevent chattering or breaking.
- Rigid Fixtures for Roughing Operations: Maximize roughing operations by ensuring a rigid fixture or setup, especially when machining harder materials like stainless steel.
- Metal Removal Rates Influence Machining Strategy: A machining method with a higher metal removal rate may not always be the most efficient if adjustments are needed due to variables like material properties.
- Balance Efficiency and Cycle Time: While efficiency is important, spending too much time optimizing can result in minimal cycle time savings. Balance optimization efforts with practical results.
- Reduce Cycle Time in Production: In a production environment, reducing cycle time is crucial. However, in a job shop making one-off parts, focusing on cycle time might be wasteful.
- Be Proactive in Programming: As a programmer, be proactive and provide detailed setup sheets with notes on everything to watch for and special instructions to prevent issues during the process.
- Add Qualifying Features for Operators: Include additional qualifying features and M0 program stops in your setup sheets to help operators check their work and prevent mistakes.
- Deburr Features in the Machine: Add tools to deburr every feature on your part during machining rather than relying on operators, which can prevent shipping parts with burrs.
- Predict and Prevent Issues: Try to predict what can go wrong during the process and add preventive measures in your setup sheets to reduce machine downtime and scrap.
- Simplify Processes for Operators: Create simple and easy-to-follow processes to reduce the risk of human error and guesswork, adopting methods like poke-yoke (mistake-proofing).
- Understand Tooling Thoroughly: Study different types of tools, their uses, strengths, and weaknesses to make informed decisions in your programming.
- Research Tools for Efficiency: Spending time researching tools helps you understand which ones are more efficient, control chip formation, and provide better finish.
- Evaluate Tool Cost vs. Performance: Consider whether the cheapest or most expensive tool is worth the price for the work it's doing and if it allows you to run your machine to its potential.
- Use Versatile Tools for Cost Savings: Versatile tools like those with universal coatings or inserts for multiple materials can save money by reducing the need to stock multiple tool types.
- Collaborate with Tooling Engineers: Stay informed about new technology by collaborating with tooling engineers to maintain a competitive advantage.
- Learn from Others' Programming Styles: Observe how others program and process projects, ask them why they made certain choices to understand their thought processes and learn from their knowledge.
- Expand Your Mind by Thinking Outside the Box: Avoid tunnel vision and singular patterns by incorporating good habits from unconventional thinkers to enhance your knowledge and expertise quickly.

tips.title: GibbsCAM Tech Tip: How to Create a Trochoidal Toolpath
tips.text:
- Depth Matters in Dummy Operation: In the dummy operation, depth is crucial as it directly affects the finish pass. The depth should be set accurately to ensure proper material removal for the final cut.
- Use of Stepover in Trochoidal Toolpath: The stepover for the trochoidal toolpath is set to 09, which corresponds to 6% of the cutter diameter. This ensures adequate material removal while maintaining efficiency.
- Tool Selection for Trochoidal Cut: A 1/8 inch solid carbide end mill is used for the trochoidal cut at an RPM of 14,500 and a feed rate of 14.7.

tips.title: Episode 2: Chip Thinning
tips.text:
- Avoiding Rubbing by Managing Chip Thinning: Reducing the feed rate or step over too much can cause rubbing due to chip thinning, which makes chips thinner and increases the risk of tool wear.
- Calculate Feed Rate to Offset Chip Thinning: To avoid rubbing, calculate the required feed rate based on target chip load and cut width to account for chip thinning.
- Use Feeds and Speeds Calculators for Chip Thinning: Utilize feeds and speeds calculators like G Wizard to automatically account for chip thinning and ensure optimal cutting parameters.
- Adjust Feed Rate for Chip Thinning: When not making a full slotting cut, increase the feed rate and RPMs to maintain chip thickness. The adjusted chip load should be higher (e.g., 35,000 instead of 28,000) to avoid thinning.
- Chip Thinning in Circular Cuts: Chip thinning occurs in circular cuts with tools like ballnose cutters or round inserts, requiring adjustments for both cut width and depth.
- Use Calculators for Chip Thinning Adjustments: Adjusting speeds and feeds manually for chip thinning is complex; use spreadsheets or feeds and speeds calculators to simplify the process.
- Avoid Excessive Feed Rate Reduction: Reducing feed rate and cut width too much can lead to rubbing, which shortens tool life. Ensure rates are high enough to avoid rubbing.
- Benefits of Proper Chip Thinning Adjustment: Properly adjusting for chip thinning can improve tool life and reduce cycle times.

tips.title: Climb vs Conventional Milling
tips.text:
- Climb vs Conventional Milling: In climb milling, the cutter head moves into the piece and takes a big chunk at the start, moving down. In conventional milling, the cutter head moves away from the piece on the upstroke of the metal.
- Backlash Consideration in Manual Milling: Climb milling can be tough on manual machines due to backlash, which can pull the work into the cutter head and cause a bad finish or damage the piece.
- Conventional Milling on Manual Machines: For manual machines, conventional milling is preferred to avoid the issues caused by backlash.

tips.title: Conventional vs Climb Milling On A CNC Machine - CNC Basics – WorkBee
tips.text:
- Conventional Milling Chip Recut: In conventional milling, chips are carried upward of the cup, resulting in chip recut, extra heat buildup, and reduced tool life.
- Climb Milling Chip Formation: In climb milling, chips are cut starting at maximum width and reducing to zero width, which can reduce tool life up to 50%.
- Conventional Milling Deflection: Conventional milling puts greater force on the tool, causing larger deflection parallel to the feed direction, which has minimal effect on part geometry.
- Climb Milling Deflection: Climb milling deflection is smaller than conventional but can affect part geometry due to perpendicular chip formation.
- Rough Cutting Recommendation: It is normally best to rough cut using climb milling due to smaller deflection or use greater pass steps.
- Finishing Pass Selection: For finishing passes, use conventional milling if deflection is going to be troublesome for part geometry.
- Conventional Milling Force Direction: In conventional milling, the tool takes the largest cut meaning the material makes an upward force on the workpiece.
- Climb Milling Force Direction: In climb milling, the forces act downwards which helps to stabilize the part being cut.
- Tool Path Selection in Conventional Milling: When slotting such as a profile cut, the tool will be conventional cut 50% of the time and climb cutting the other 30%.
- Climb Milling and Chip Load: Climb milling can increase the chip load due to backlash if the climb force is strong enough.

tips.title: How to Get PERFECT Speeds and Feeds for Any Material in CNC Machining?
tips.text:
- Experience-Based Speeds and Feeds: From experience cutting always pushing the limits, keeping track of MRR and minutes in cut for each tool.
- Utilize Other People's Experience: Talk to tool reps, designers, and pick their brains about tests they have done.
- Use Inventor's Recommendations as Baseline: Document what tool inventors say and use it as a baseline to improve upon.
- Pushing Speeds and Feeds for Hard Materials: Examples of machining titanium, hastelloy, monnell, a286, incannel with high speeds and feeds.
- High Speeds and Feeds for Aluminum: Roughing aluminum at 800 inches per minute, challenging conventional wisdom.
- Bank and Use Documented Information: Bank information on surface foot, chip loads, and use it in the shop with the same tools and techniques.

tips.title: Deep Pocket Finishing with a Back Draft Cutter – 3D Finish Milling Tips
tips.text:
- Backdraft Cutter for Deep Pocket Finishing: Use a backdraft or bullnose cutter for deep pockets with tapered walls. Solid carbide end mills are suitable for shallow, straight-walled pockets.
- Minimizing Deflection: A backdraft tool engages a small amount of the insert, holding tool pressure to a minimum and reducing deflection.
- Track Profiling Routine: Use track profiling routines (race track, plunge track, or plunge finishing) for better control and straightness in pocket walls.
- Consistent Surface Finish: A backdraft cutter provides a very straight wall and nice surface finish, allowing the same tool to be used for both walls and floor.
- Slower Feed Rate for Floor: Use a slower feed rate with the same tool to achieve a nice finish on the floor of the pocket.
- Nice Looking Blend: Using the same tool for both walls and floor generally allows for a nice looking blend or transition at the intersection.

tips.title: Fusion 360 CAM Tip: How to Contain 2D Adaptive Toolpaths | FF132
tips.text:
- Selecting Contours for 2D Adaptive Toolpaths: When setting up a 2D adaptive toolpath, select contours instead of faces to avoid unwanted areas in the toolpath.
- Updating Toolpath Selections: To add areas to a selected contour for a toolpath, hover over the area and click to add it.
- Setting Correct Z-Plane for Toolpaths: Ensure the correct z-plane is set when using natural contour selection to avoid machining into unintended areas.
- Modify Stock Setup in Fusion 360: To fix the stock setup issue, use 'Edit Geometry' to check stock contours and override what is considered as stock to machine. This allows you to pick a profile that represents your part accurately.
- Limit Tool Passes with Stock Contours: Using stock contours in Fusion 360 can limit tool passes by overriding the stock to machine, which is useful for avoiding areas like pre-existing holes.
- Handling Curve Bosses in Stock Setup: When dealing with curve bosses, manually highlight and expand the selection to cover the full periphery of the part since Fusion 360 may not automatically select a natural full plane profile.

tips.title: 5-Axis Made Easy -  Parts 1, 2 and 3
tips.text:
- Reduce Setups with 5-Axis Machining: Using 5-axis machining can reduce setups from four to two, decreasing the chance of mistakes and scrap.
- Dovetail Fixture for Secure Clamping: A dovetail fixture allows secure clamping of the part using minimal material, cutting only an eighth of an inch deep.
- Five-Axis Benefits: 5-axis machining increases accuracy, shortens cycle times, and reduces scrap by up to 21 percent.
- Configuration Considerations: Choosing the right machine and rotary product combination is crucial for versatility and success.
- Workholding Challenges in 5-Axis Machining: Standard mill vices are often inadequate for 5-axis machining, requiring specialized workholding solutions.
- Tooling Challenges in 5-Axis Machining: Standard length weld and style tool holders are often impractical for 5-axis machining, necessitating specific tool holder choices.
- Programming Requirements for 5-Axis Machining: Effective and efficient programming in 5-axis machining requires a CAM system capable of handling multiple angles.
- Choosing a Rotary Table Size: The size of the rotary table should accommodate the workpiece, ensuring it fits within the diameter of the rotary platter.
- HA-5C Rotary Products for Smaller Parts: For smaller parts that can fit in a 5C collet, HA-5C rotary products are available with options like pneumatic collet closers and manual chucks.
- Variety of Rotary Tables for Larger Workpieces: For larger workpieces, Haas offers rotary tables with platters ranging from 160 millimeters to 600 millimeters in diameter.
- HRT A5 and A6 Rotary Products for Round Workpieces: Consider HRT A5 or A6 rotary products for round workpieces, which come with standard spindle noses for direct chuck fitting.
- Trunnion vs TRT Design: The trunnion design supports the tilt axis on both ends, allowing a larger part swing diameter compared to the TRT design.
- HAAS UMC and Five Series Models: HAAS offers dedicated 5-axis models like the UMC series and five-axis series, where the rotary table can be removed to return the machine to a three-axis configuration.
- VF and TR Series Options: HAAS VF series models come with options like high-speed machining, dynamic work offsets, and tool center point control necessary for 5-axis machining.
- Extended Clearance Options: HAAS offers low profile table and column riser options to add clearance on VF3/VF4 and VF6-VF11 size machines respectively, without adding Z-axis travel.
- Workholding Considerations: When installing rotary products, workholding like vices may need sub-plates or risers underneath them to accommodate the larger spindle nose to table distance.
- Floor Space and Usable Table Space: Consider the floor space occupied by the mill and the usable mill table space when choosing a rotary model, as larger rotaries can reduce usable table space.
- Lifting Capacity Requirement: A larger rotary requires a larger lifting capacity to get it on and off the machine.
- TRT-100 Rotary Recommendation: For small parts, the TRT-100 is recommended due to its five-inch work envelope and ample mill table space left over for a mill vise.
- TR-200Y Rotary Recommendation: For work envelopes up to 8 inches, the TR-200Y is the most versatile option, allowing for multiple vises and flexibility for both 3-axis and 5-axis work.
- UMC Series Recommendation: For workpieces larger than 8 inches, the UMC series is recommended due to its 500 millimeter diameter platter providing room for two standard six-inch mill vises.
- Dynamic Work Offset and Tool Center Point Control Option: This option allows for part location in the machine to vary from model to model, simplifying setup and reducing setup time.
- Wireless Intuitive Probing System Recommendation: Highly recommended for accurately locating the machine rotary zero points and setting tool length and work offsets quickly, easily, and accurately.
- High-Speed Machining Option Requirement: Required for simultaneous 5-axis tool paths and necessary for machining 3D parts.
- High Speed Machining Feed Rate Adjustment: High speed machining adjusts the feed rate based on the length of block, change in direction, and need to stay on the programmed path, similar to driving a windy road where you learn optimal braking and acceleration.
- Rotary Size Selection Based on Part Size: When selecting a rotary for multi-axis machining, the part size dictates the rotary size.
- Simplified Rotary Installation with DWO and TCPC: Using DWO (Dynamic Work Offset) and TCPC (Tool Center Point Compensation), rotary installation on a three-axis Haas mill is easier, eliminating manual calculations and reducing the need to frequently update computer geometry.
- Workholding Adjustment: The part needs to be held in a vise instead of a rotary fixture plate due to coordinate height differences.
- Dynamic Work Offset (DWO) and Tool Center Point Control (TCPC): Using DWO and TCPC automatically offsets the program in machine space, regardless of rotary moves or angles.
- Machine Rotary Zero Point (MRZP): The machine rotary zero point (MRZP) is defined by two coordinates for each axis and is crucial for setting up a two-axis rotary on a mill.
- Check Tilt Axis Flatness: Ensure the tilt axis is flat before proceeding with setup.
- Reset Tool Changer Offset: Use the insert key to set TC offset after zero returning the axis.
- Avoid Tool Changer Interference: Set user positions for tool change travel limits to avoid interference with tall fixtures or rotary tables.
- Set Z-Axis Tool Change Mid Position: Ensure the z-axis moves first in the tool change mid position sequence if necessary.
- Use MRZP Probatronian Template: Select the appropriate MRZP Probatronian template for your rotary model during setup.
- Using Probing for Machine Rotary Zero: The machine can probe the center bore of the rotary and get the X, Y, and Z coordinates to find the C-axis location. It also probes the platter in Z and rotates the tilt axis to 90 and -90 degrees to find the center of X or Y.
- Dynamic Work Offsets for Easy Setup: Using dynamic work offsets and tool center point control makes setting up a five-axis job as easy as setting up a three-axis job.

tips.title: Fast Hole and Wire EDM | Learn to Burn
tips.text:
- Material Selection for Fast Hole EDM: Brass is typically used for steel and aluminum, while copper is used for carbide and very hard materials.
- Fast Hole EDM vs. Carbide Drilling: Fast hole EDM is significantly faster than carbide drilling, especially for smaller drills and hardened steel.
- Avoiding Standing Bosses in EDM Holes: Better fast hole EDM drills have multiple flushing spots to ensure the center cuts out any standing bosses.
- Importance of Flushing in EDM: Flushing is crucial in EDM as it helps remove debris and improves the speed and effectiveness of the burn.
- Deionized Water in Fast Hole EDM: Using deionized water in fast hole EDM allows for faster burns compared to thicker EDM oils.
- Preventing Rust in Fast Hole EDM: Using deionized water helps prevent rust on blocks by allowing for quicker hole making and block removal.
- Fast Hole Diameter Range: You can make fast holes down to a 7 mm diameter up to a 6 mm diameter, which is like a 0.236 inch hole.
- Importance of Flatness in Setup: It is important to ensure the block is as flat as possible when setting up for fast holes.
- Centering Technique for Fast Holes: To center the block, touch each side and split the difference to find the center accurately.
- Edge Drilling Consideration: When drilling holes on an edge, there's a risk of the drill wandering, but it is unlikely to be a problem with fast hole technology.
- Fast Hole Cycle Time: A typical hole with fast hole technology takes about a minute or two to go through a block that is about an inch and a half thick.
- Manual Machine Mistakes: Mistakes are more common on manual machines compared to CNC machines.
- Wire EDM Standard Wire Diameter: Most people use a 10,000 diameter wire for wire EDM, which covers a large variety of tooling needs.
- Wire Size Range: The wire size range for the machine is from 2000 to 14000 diameter, with 10th out wire being commonly used.
- Diamond Guides Calibration: Diamond guides need to be calibrated every time they are changed.
- Wire EDM Maintenance: Wire EDM machines require maintenance of consumable wire, diamond guides, and carbide contactors.
- Wire EDM Angle Limitation: The angle limit for tipping the U and V head, as well as the X and Y head on a wire EDM machine is up to 45 degrees.
- Wire Tension for Different Brass Hardness: Soft brass can go up to 45 degrees, half-hard brass up to 25 degrees, and hard brass up to 10 degrees in tension.
- Wire EDM Fluid Options: Most people use deionized water, but dielectric fluid can be used for better precision and accuracy at the cost of speed.
